summary:
MISSION AUTOPSY: The Last Telemetry is a sci-fi space systems engineering and forensic investigation simulation game developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Stepping into NASA Mission Control, players investigate the sudden blackout of deep-space probe ASTER-9 during an asteroid rendezvous. Guided by Nova, an AI-augmented cybernetic companion, players scrub multi-channel black box telemetry for tracking bus voltage, battery freezing, and solar dropouts to pin anomalous evidence. Guesswork is never enough; investigators must scientifically prove their root-cause hypothesis before a NASA review board to unlock redesign funding.

Players then re-engineer the spacecraft in an interactive systems lab, balancing critical trade-offs between mass, power architectures, thermal insulation, and a strict $65M budget. The redesigned craft is stress-tested in a real-time 3D orbital flight simulation through the freezing asteroid shadow.

Featuring a sleek anime sci-fi interface, the game supports both solo challenges and co-operative role-based multiplayer (Telemetry Analyst, Systems Engineer, Electrical Specialist, Medical Officer, and Flight Director). It merges real aerospace trade-offs with thrilling investigative gameplay, proving that “Every failure leaves a signal.”
details:
MISSION AUTOPSY — The Last Telemetry

Project Details | NASA International Space Apps Challenge 2026

MISSION AUTOPSY — The Last Telemetry is a web-based investigation and survival game that puts players in the role of a spacecraft investigation and engineering team. When a spacecraft starts to fail, players must read its telemetry, find the real cause of each fault, decide what to fix first, and carry out repairs before the vehicle's condition collapses. It turns the reasoning that real mission teams use into an experience anyone with a web browser can play.

What does it do, and how does it work?

The game recreates the core loop of a real spacecraft failure investigation. Every mission follows the same reasoning path:

- Investigate: The ship screen shows a visualization of the spacecraft with damage hotspots (Electrical System, Propulsion, Communication Array, Navigation, Life Support, Thermal Control, Computer System) marked in red. A hotspot shows that something is wrong but not why.

- Analyze telemetry: Each hotspot is backed by real-style telemetry such as power output, battery voltage, temperature, and current load. Players read these values to work out which subsystem is failing and why, the way flight controllers reason from data rather than direct observation.

- Diagnose: Players submit which system is affected, the likely cause, the severity, and the priority action. The system rates the answer as Correct, Partially Correct, or Incorrect. Only a correct diagnosis unlocks the matching repair.

- Repair: Each fault type has its own mini-game: Cable Connection for electrical failures, Power Routing, Propulsion Calibration, Cooling System Management, Antenna Alignment, Sensor Calibration, System Reboot, and Navigation Reconfiguration.

- Manage the clock and ship condition: A mission timer runs from the moment the emergency begins. Six indicators (Hull Integrity, Power Stability, Propulsion, Life Support, Communication, and Navigation) react to every fault. Faults follow cause-and-effect chains, so an unresolved electrical failure can disrupt power distribution and then knock out communication.

Two game modes

- Story Mode: A guided campaign that opens with a comic-style story about the ASTER-9 spacecraft, then progresses through six episodes on a Space Map: ASTER-9 (tutorial), Solar Frontier (energy faults), Silent Orbit (communication), Iron Horizon (propulsion), Deep Space (multiple subsystems), and Final Signal (critical, cascading failures).

- Co-op Mode — Last Stand: Up to four players join a lobby with an invitation code (for example NOVA-7X29), choose from 10 unique Agents, and work together to keep a spacecraft alive as long as possible. Damage escalates through phases, from Minor Failure up to Deep Space Crisis, based on survival time, active damage, ship condition, and the team's repair success, not just elapsed time.

Agents and the NOVA companion

The 10 playable Agents belong to four engineering roles: Telemetry Analyst, Electrical Engineer, Mechanical & Propulsion Engineer, and Systems Engineer. Each role gives an advantage (extra analysis hints, faster electrical or engine repairs, or detection of linked faults) without making any single Agent mandatory. Roles can repeat on a team, but each Agent can be picked only once. NOVA, the in-game AI companion, introduces the game, asks for the player's name, runs the tutorial, warns players when ship condition worsens, gives hints when they are stuck, and delivers a debrief after every mission. Its messages are kept short so they never block gameplay. After each game, a debrief shows diagnostic accuracy, repair efficiency, survival time, final ship condition, and score. Planned global, weekly, and friends leaderboards, plus a weekly challenge in which everyone plays the same scenario, add replay value and fair competition.

What benefits does it have?

- Makes spacecraft operations understandable: Telemetry, subsystems, and fault diagnosis are usually hidden behind technical documents. The game lets players learn them by doing, starting from zero knowledge.

- Trains real analytical skills: Players practice reading data, forming a hypothesis, checking it, and prioritizing under time pressure, which are skills that transfer to science, engineering, and everyday problem-solving.

- Teaches systems thinking: Because one fault can spread to other subsystems, players learn to look for root causes instead of just treating symptoms.

- Builds teamwork: In Co-op Mode, players must divide work, communicate, and coordinate tasks that depend on each other, just as real mission control teams do.

- Learning without fear of failure: Mistakes cost time and add some risk, but first errors are penalized lightly so players learn from them instead of giving up.

- Accessible anywhere: It runs in a web browser, so it needs no installation, special hardware, or paid software, and works for classrooms, clubs, and home players.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Our goal is to bring students and the general public closer to the work that keeps space missions alive. The primary audience is secondary and university students interested in space, engineering, and technology. The secondary audience is casual gamers who enjoy puzzle, simulation, and cooperative games. We want players to finish a mission understanding three ideas: spacecraft health is judged through data, failures rarely have a single obvious cause, and recovering a mission depends on people working together. Connecting these ideas to a memorable story can spark curiosity about space careers and STEM learning. Because the mission and damage systems are modular, teachers and the community can add new scenarios over time, including ones inspired by real NASA mission themes. Playtesting will measure whether new players can understand telemetry, diagnosis, and repair without excessive help, and we will use the results to tune difficulty and learning flow.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

The game is designed as a full web application with a server-authoritative multiplayer backend:

- Frontend: React / Next.js

- Programming language: TypeScript

- Styling: Tailwind CSS / CSS Modules

- Animation: Framer Motion / GSAP

- 2D rendering: HTML Canvas

- 3D rendering: Three.js

- Backend: Node.js

- Real-time multiplayer: Socket.IO / WebSocket

- Database: PostgreSQL

- Cache / sessions: Redis (optional)

- Deployment: Web hosting with WebSocket support

- Hardware: None required; any device with a modern web browser

Architecture

- Game client (frontend): Renders every screen, animation, telemetry panel, and repair mini-game, and sends player actions to the server.

- Game server (backend): Manages lobbies, Agent selection, timers, the damage system, diagnosis validation, repair tasks, ship condition, and synchronization of all players.

- Database: Stores player profiles, Agent data, Story progress, Co-op results, leaderboards, and weekly challenges.

In Co-op Mode the server is the single source of truth. When a player finishes a repair, the server checks that the task is still active, that the player may perform it, and that the mini-game result is valid, then updates ship condition and broadcasts it to everyone. Clients never decide repair results, timers, or scores, which prevents cheating and keeps all players in the same state. Communication is event-based (for example lobby:join, agent:lock, damage:new, repair:complete, ship:state, and game:results).

How is your project creative?

- It turns investigation into gameplay: Most space games are about flying or fighting. MISSION AUTOPSY is about being the engineer who figures out what went wrong, using data as the main clue, like a detective story set in mission control.

- Repairs match the fault: Instead of a generic repair button, each failure type has its own mini-game, so fixing an antenna feels different from rerouting power or calibrating an engine.

- Failures behave like a real system: Damage spreads through believable cause-and-effect chains, and Co-op escalation adapts to how the team is performing, so every session plays out differently.

- Story and character bring the science to life: A comic-style opening, an AI companion with personality, and 10 original Agents give players an emotional reason to care about technical concepts.

- A distinctive visual identity: The game uses an anime-inspired science-fiction style with holographic, tactical mission-control panels and fully original characters and assets. Color has meaning: cyan for normal information, yellow for warnings, red for critical damage, and green for successful repairs, so players can read the ship's status at a glance.

What factors did your team consider?

- Real mission history: The design is grounded in how real failures were investigated. The Apollo 13 Review Board report and the Columbia Accident Investigation Board report showed that failures involve chains of technical and human factors. The NASA Systems Engineering Handbook informed how subsystems depend on each other, and CCSDS material informed how telemetry is presented.

- Learning design: We used the MDA (Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics) framework, flow theory to match challenge to skill, and gamification research to keep players engaged. Concepts are introduced gradually and revisited in harder missions.

- Accuracy and honesty: Telemetry values, repair durations, and damage scaling are starting values that will be tested and balanced. Any claim of realistic simulation will be checked against credible technical references.

- Fair and balanced Agents: Abilities give strategic options without making any Agent required, and selection rules keep teams flexible.

- Usability: Important information must be easy to find, telemetry must be readable, animations must not interrupt play, the interface must work on different screen sizes, and players should understand ship status without opening many menus.

- Security and reliability: All important actions are validated on the server, lobby codes are hard to guess and join attempts are limited, timers use server timestamps, only validated scores are stored, and disconnected players get a reconnection grace period.

- Privacy: Player name input is validated and no unnecessary personal information is collected.

- Feasibility for a small team: Development follows a nine-phase roadmap and a focused Minimum Viable Product (one ASTER-9 mission with two to three hotspots and one to two mini-games, plus a basic four-player Co-op scenario). Features such as voice chat, public matchmaking, and cosmetics are postponed. Risks such as scope creep, asset workload, unstable multiplayer, and device performance each have a planned mitigation.
